Here we are given a data set $P$ consisting of points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space and the task is to find $k$ centers $S$ such that \[
  \text{cost}(P,S):=\sum_{p\in P} \min_{c\in S}\|p-c\|^2  \]
is minimized, where $\|x\|=(\sum_{i=1}^d x_i^2)^{1/2}$ denotes the length of a vector.

nodes.name: $\ensuremath{\varepsilon}$-Coreset

nodes.statement: Recall that X^S,h is given by the following expression: X^S,h :=& fracsum_i in [m]g_i w_q_i (uqS,hi - uqS,h-1i)textnormalcost(P,S). Since X^S,h is a sum of independent centered Gaussians (using Creffact: gaussian), it is also a centered Gaussian with variance: &Var[X^S,h] = (1/textnormalcost(P,S))^2 cdot sum_i in [m] w_q_i^2 (u_i^S, h -u_i^S, h-1)^2 . Recall that the net vector u^S,h is an m-dimensional vector whose entries approximate the cost of points in B(S) cap Omega with respect to S (see Crefdef: clustering-nets) where B(S) is the set of clusters in band b and type t. It follows from the definition of u^S,h that, [(i)] item If q_i in B(S) then, |u_i^S,h - u_i^S,h-1| leq |u_i^S,h - u_i^S| + |u_i^S,h-1 - u_i^S| leq 2^-h textnormalerr(q_i, S) + 2^-(h-1) textnormalerr(q_i, S)lesssim 2^-h textnormalerr(q_i, S). item If q_i notin B(S) then u_i^S,h = u_i^S,h-1 = 0. nodes.statement: Fix a center x and let r:= |I(x)|. Without loss of generality, we can assume that r geq 2 (otherwise, the bound holds trivially). For convenience, we re-index the clusters so that the set of clusters that interact with x is I(x) = \C_1, ldots, C_r\, and such that the clusters are indexed in the increasing order of the distance of their centers from x. We show that all clusters except possibly C_1 have cost Omega(beta ensuremathOPT_k) with respect to S. This then implies the desired bound. Using the guarantee of Creflem: approxstability on the distance between centers a_i, a_j of stable instances and the triangle inequality, we get (beta ensuremathOPT_k)/2|C_j| leq textnormalcost(a_1, a_j) leq 2(textnormalcost(a_1, x) + textnormalcost(a_j,x)) leq 4textnormalcost(a_j,x) leq 64textnormalcost(a_j,S). The last inequality above uses the fact that x is an approximate nearest center to a_j (see Crefdef: interaction). Rearranging we get textnormalcost(a_j,S) geq (beta ensuremathOPT_k)/(128 |C_j|). Since the cost of the center of C_j is high, we can argue that the cost of C_j is lower bounded by Omega(|C_j| textnormalcost(a_j, S)). This is formalized by the following claim whose proof is in Crefapp: missing-proofs. Let S be a set of k centers. Suppose that C_j is a cluster whose center a_j satisfies textnormalcost(a_j,S) geq 32Delta_j; then textnormalcost(C_j,S) geq tfrac16 |C_j| textnormalcost(a_j,S). By Crefdef: interaction we have textnormalcost(a_j,x) geq 32 Delta_j. This together with and Creflem: cost-from-center gives textnormalcost(C_j,S) geq tfrac16 |C_j| textnormalcost(a_j,S) geq tfrac1768 beta ensuremathOPT_k.qedhere

Suppose instead that t geq 6. We proceed similarly as in Creflem: easy-var to obtain, Var[X^S,h]&lesssim (1/textnormalcost(P,S))^2 cdot 2^-2h cdot sum_q in B(S) cap Omega w_q^2 textnormalerr(q,S)^2. Using the definition of textnormalerr(q,S) (see Crefdef: clustering-nets) we now obtain: sum_q in B(S) cap Omega w_q^2 cdot textnormalerr(q,S)^2 lesssim sum_q in B(S)cap Omega w_q^2 (textnormalcost(q,S) textnormalcost(q,A) + textnormalcost(q,S) Delta_q + textnormalcost(q,A)^2 + Delta_q^2). Next observe that by Creflem: weight-bound, the weights satisfy w_q textnormalcost(q,A) lesssim k textnormalcost(C_j, A)/m and also w_q Delta_q lesssim k Delta_j |C_j|/m) lesssim k textnormalcost(C_j, A)/m) given by Creflem: weight-bound. Since each cluster C_j in B(S) is in band b, we have textnormalcost(C_j, A) lesssim 2^b T. Thus we get, Gamma := sum_q in B(S) cap Omega w_q^2 textnormalerr(q,S)^2 lesssim (k 2^b T)/m cdot sum_q in B(S) cap Omega w_q (textnormalcost(q,S) + textnormalcost(q,A) + Delta_q). nodes.raw_latex:
We will argue that for the $1$-mean problem, any coreset must have $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-2})$ points. The claim then follows by adding multiple copies of the $1$-mean instance with an arbitrarily large separation.

 Our instance is the $n$-dimensional simplex, where $n=\varepsilon^{-2}$. More concretely, the points in $A$ correspond to the standard unit basis of $\mathbb{R}^{n}.$
Note that $\mu(A) = \frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}$ and $\sum_{p\in A} \|p-\mu(A)\|^2 = n-1$.

Let $\Omega$ be the designated coreset with non-negative weight function $w:\Omega\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$.
We must have $w(\Omega):=\sum_{p\in \Omega} w_p\geq (1-\varepsilon)\cdot n$, as otherwise the cost of far away center cannot be well approximated.
Consider the point $s:=(\sum_{p\in \Omega}p)/\|\sum_{p\in \Omega}p\|$. Notice that 
We have 
\[\|p-s\|^2 = 2-2/\sqrt{|\Omega|} \text{for any $p\in \Omega$, and }  \|q-s\|^2 = 2
\text{ for every } q\in A\setminus \Omega,
\]
and thus  $\textnormal{cost}(A,s) = 2(n-\sqrt{|\Omega|})$.
At the same time, we know that 
\[\textnormal{cost}(\Omega,s) = w(\Omega)\cdot \left(2-2|\Omega|^{-1/2}\right)\leq 2(1+\varepsilon)\cdot\left(n-\sqrt{|\Omega|} + \sqrt{|\Omega|}-n|\Omega|^{-1/2}\right),\]
and thus
\[\textnormal{cost}(A,s)-\textnormal{cost}(\Omega,s)\geq -\varepsilon\cdot 2(n-|\Omega|^{1/2}) + 2(1+\varepsilon)\cdot (n|\Omega|^{-1/2}-|\Omega|^{1/2}).\]
With some straightforward, but tedious calculation, this term is greater than $\varepsilon\cdot 2(n-|\Omega|^{1/2})$ whenever
$|\Omega|<\left(-\varepsilon^{-1}/2 + \sqrt{\varepsilon^{-2}/4+(1+\varepsilon)\cdot \varepsilon^{-2}}\right)^2\approx 0.61\cdot  \varepsilon^{-2}$.

Therefore, any $1$-mean coreset on $A$ must have size at least $0.61\ensuremath{\varepsilon}^{-2}$. Let $A'$ be a set of $k$ copies of $A$, placed arbitrarily far away from each other. We argue that a coreset for $k$-means on $A'$ must be a coreset for $1$-mean on most of the copies. 

First, the weight of each copy of $A$ is preserved, up to $(1\pm \ensuremath{\varepsilon})$: consider a set of centers $S$ where each copy of $A$ but one gets one center at the origin, and the last copy gets a center far away (say, distance $kn^2$). This copy will dictate the entire cost of the instance, and therefore its weight must be well approximated.

Preserving the weight implies that, for each simplex, the cost of clustering it to its origin is preserved. Suppose now that $|\Omega| \leq \frac{k(10\ensuremath{\varepsilon})^{-2}}{100}$. Then, at least $9k/10$ copies get fewer than $0.61\cdot (10\ensuremath{\varepsilon})^{-2}$ points: let $A_1, ..., A_{k'}$ be those copies. In $A_i$, the cost of center $s_i$ (defined previously as the average of coreset points in $A_i$) will be underestimated by $10 \ensuremath{\varepsilon} \cdot 2(n-\sqrt{|\Omega \cap S_i|}) \geq 10\ensuremath{\varepsilon} (2n-2\sqrt{n}) \geq 10\ensuremath{\varepsilon} n$. For each other copy, the cost of clustering to the origin is overestimated by at most $\ensuremath{\varepsilon} n$, since the weight is preserved. 


Consider therefore the set of centers consisting the origins and the $s_i$. Its cost is $k/10 n + 9k/10 \cdot 2n- \sum_{i=1}^{k'}\sqrt{|\Omega \cap A_i|} \leq k/10 n + 9kn/5 \leq 2k n$. 
The previous discussion shows that the estimation error from $\Omega$ is at least $9k/10 \cdot 10\ensuremath{\varepsilon} n - k/10 \cdot \ensuremath{\varepsilon} n$. This is at least $8k \ensuremath{\varepsilon} n $, which is strictly more than an $\ensuremath{\varepsilon}$ fraction of the cost of the full instance. Hence, such a small $\Omega$ cannot be a coreset, which concludes the proof.

nodes.statement: Let C=\mu_1,mu_2,ldots,mu_k\ be an optimal solution with induced clusters \C_1,ldots,C_k\ and let Delta = textnormalcost(P,C). We claim that C, where mu_i is weighted by |C_i| is the desired coreset. Consider some solution S. We first observe that if the points in C_i are served by a single center in s_iin S, then textnormalcost(C_i,s_i) = textnormalcost(C_i,mu_i) + |C_i|textnormalcost(mu_i,s_i) due to Lemma . Therefore, for any solution S where each cluster is served by a single center, the cost is exactly preserved. Next, suppose that some cluster C_i is served by at least two centers s,s'in S. Then there must exist two clusters C_a and C_b that are served by the same center s''. For any cluster C_i, we have & leftvert textnormalcost(C_i,S) - (|C_i|textnormalcost(mu_i,S) + textnormalcost(C_i, mu_i)) rightvert = biggvert sum_pin C_i textnormalcost(p,S) - (textnormalcost(mu_i,S) + textnormalcost(p,mu_i)) biggvert\\ &leq sum_pin C_i varepsilon/2cdot textnormalcost(p,S) + (8/varepsilon)cdot textnormalcost(p,mu_i) = varepsilon/2cdot textnormalcost(C_i,S) + (8/varepsilon)cdot textnormalcost(C_i,C). Summed over all clusters, this ensures | textnormalcost(P,S) - (sum_i |C_i|textnormalcost(mu_i,S) + textnormalcost(P, C)) | leq varepsilon/2cdot textnormalcost(P,S) + (8/varepsilon)cdot ensuremathOPT_k. We use the stability property to bound ensuremathOPT_k. Without loss of generality, assume that \|mu_a - s''\| leq \|mu_b-s''\|. Combined with the properties of beta-stable instances ( Creflem: approxstability), this ensures textnormalcost(mu_b,S) > textnormalcost(mu_b,mu_a)/4 geq betacdot OPT_k/(8|C_b|). Therefore, we get: ensuremathOPT_k &leq 8 |C_b|textnormalcost(mu_b, S)/beta leq (ensuremathvarepsilon^2/64) cdot (sum_i |C_i|textnormalcost(mu_i,S) + textnormalcost(P, C))\\ &leq (ensuremathvarepsilon^2/64) big(textnormalcost(P, S) + bigvert textnormalcost(P,S) - big(sum_i |C_i|textnormalcost(mu_i,S) + textnormalcost(P, C)big) bigvertbig). The argument is very reliant on the worst-case lower bound construction by \cite{HLW23}.
We will only describe the properties that are necessary to ensure that their lower bound applies to a perturbation-resilient instance and encourage the reader to refer to their proof for details.
The simplest variant of their lower bound assumes that $\varepsilon^{-1} = k^{1/4}.$
The points $P$ are split into $k/2$ groups with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The groups have equal size $\Theta(k)$,
    \item Two points in the same group have pairwise distance $\Theta(1)$,
    \item Two points in different groups have pairwise distance $\Theta(\varepsilon^{-1})$.
\end{enumerate}



Notice that this instance would be perturbation-resilient for $\alpha\in \Theta(k^{1/4})$, if we had $k$ groups, each inducing a cluster.
To create a perturbation-resilient point set, we introduce a modified copy $P'$ of $P$ located at an arbitrary distance with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The groups have equal size $\Theta(k)$,
    \item Two points in the same group have pairwise distance $\Theta(1)$,
    \item Two points in different groups have pairwise distance $\Theta(\alpha)$.
\end{enumerate}

Observe that now the groups of $P\cup P'$ are the clusters of an optimal solution and that the instance is $\Omega(\alpha)$-perturbation stable. We further observe that if we serve all the points of $P'$ with one center, the cost increases by roughly a factor $\Theta(\alpha^2)$.
However,  there are now $k/2$ unused centers with which $P$ becomes a worst-case instance for coresets with $\varepsilon' = \Theta(\varepsilon/\alpha^2)$. Thus, a coreset lower bound of $\Omega(k\cdot \varepsilon^{-2}\min(\sqrt{k},\varepsilon^{-2}) \cdot \alpha^{-8})$ for $\alpha$-perturbation resilient instances follows from the $\Omega(k\cdot \varepsilon^{-2}\min(\sqrt{k},\varepsilon^{-2}))$ worst case lower bound of \cite{HLW23}.

This follows from a standard application of probabilistic tail bounds.
 Fix a cluster $C_j$, and consider the random variable $W=\sum_{q \in C_j\cap \Omega} w_q$. We will show that
 \[  \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[ |W-|C_j| | > \ensuremath{\varepsilon} |C_j|] \leq \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^4/5k^4.\]
For $1 \leq i \leq m$, define the random variable $X_i$ to be the weight $w_{q_i}$ of the $i$-th sample $q_i$ if $q_i \in C_j$ and $0$ otherwise. Note that the $X_i$ are independent, $\sum_{i=1}^m  X_i = W$ and as  $w_q \mu(q)=1/m$, we have
\[\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[X_i] = \sum_{q \in C_j}  \mu(q) w_q= |C_j|/m,\] and therefore $ \mathop{\mathbb{E}}[W] = |C_j|$. 

Next, by \Cref{lem: weight-bound}, $w_q \leq 4k|C_j|/m$ for each $q\in C_j$ and thus $X_i \in [0,4k|C_j|/m]$, so that
\[ \mathop{\mathbb{E}}[X_i^2] \leq  \sum_{q \in C_j} \mu(q) w_q^2 = \sum_{q \in C_j} w_q/ m\leq \sum_{q \in C_j} 4k|C_j|/m^2  \leq 4k|C_j|^2 /m^2. \]
Let $Y_i = X_i - \mathop{\mathbb{E}}[X_i]$. Then $\sum_{i=1}^m Y_i = W- |C_j|$  and thus by Bernstein's inequality,
	\begin{align*}
		\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}} (|W -|C_j|| \geq \ensuremath{\varepsilon} |C_j|) &
		\leq 2\exp\left(\frac{-(\ensuremath{\varepsilon}|C_j|)^2/2}{4k|C_j|^2 /m + 4k\ensuremath{\varepsilon}|C_j|^2/3m}\right) \\ 
		&= 2\exp\left(- \frac{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}^2 m}{12k}\right) = 2 \left(\ensuremath{\varepsilon} / 10k\right)^4 \leq \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^4/5k^4.
	\end{align*}
where we use that $\sum_{i=1}^m \mathop{\mathbb{E}}[Y_i^2] = \sum_{i=1}^m \mathrm{Var}[X_i] \leq  \sum_{i=1}^m \mathop{\mathbb{E}}[X_i^2] \leq 4kC_j^2/m$.
The bound on $\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[P_1]$ follows by a union bound over the $k$ clusters.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{lem: approxstability}
    Let $P \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^d$ be a $\beta$-stable instance with respect to the $k$-means objective. Let $\ensuremath{\mathsf{OPT}}_k$ be the value of the optimal solution with $k$ centers. For $1 \leq \gamma \leq 1 + \beta/2$, let $\{C_1, \ldots C_k \}$ be a  $\gamma$-approximation to the optimal solution and $a_1, \ldots, a_k$ be the respective centroids of the clusters. Then for any $i, j \in[k]$ with $i \neq j$, it holds that $$\textnormal{cost}(a_i, a_j) \geq  \frac{ \beta \ensuremath{\mathsf{OPT}}_k}{2\min\left(|C_i|, |C_j|\right)}.$$

For 1 leq gamma leq 1 + beta/2, let \C_1, ldots C_k \ be a gamma-approximation to the optimal solution and a_1, ldots, a_k be the respective centroids of the clusters. Then for any i, j in[k] with i neq j, it holds that textnormalcost(a_i, a_j) geq frac beta ensuremathOPT_k2minleft(|C_i|, |C_j|right).
nodes.label: lem: approxstability

Since the solution is gamma-approximate with gamma leq 1 + beta/2, we have textnormalcost(P,A) leq (1+ beta/2) ensuremathOPT_k. By the beta-stability of the instance, ensuremathOPT_k-1 geq (1+beta) ensuremathOPT_k. Therefore, if A' = A setminus \a_i\, we have textnormalcost(P,A') geq (1+beta) ensuremathOPT_k. It follows that: fracbeta ensuremathOPT_k2 &leq textnormalcost(P,A') - textnormalcost(P,A)\\ & = textnormalcost(C_i,A') - textnormalcost(C_i, a_i) tagFor j neq i, textnormalcost(C_j, A) = textnormalcost(C_j, A') = textnormalcost(C_j,a_j)\\ & leq textnormalcost(C_i, a_j) - textnormalcost(C_i, a_i) tagtextnormalcost(p,a_j) geq textnormalcost(p, A') since a_j in A'\\ & =|C_i| cdot textnormalcost(a_i, a_j)tagUsing Creflem: centroid-fact and that a_i is the centroid of C_i. Rearranging terms proves the inequality.
nodes.raw_latex:
Fix two distinct clusters $C_i$ and $C_j$ and assume without loss of generality assume that $|C_i| \leq |C_j|$. Since the solution is $\gamma$-approximate with $\gamma \leq 1 + \beta/2$, we have $\textnormal{cost}(P,A) \leq (1+ \beta/2) \ensuremath{\mathsf{OPT}}_k$.  By the $\beta$-stability of the instance, $\ensuremath{\mathsf{OPT}}_{k-1} \geq (1+\beta) \ensuremath{\mathsf{OPT}}_k$. Therefore, if $A' = A \setminus \{a_i\}$, we have $\textnormal{cost}(P,A') \geq (1+\beta) \ensuremath{\mathsf{OPT}}_k$. It follows that: 
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{\beta \ensuremath{\mathsf{OPT}}_k}{2}  &\leq \textnormal{cost}(P,A') - \textnormal{cost}(P,A)\\
        & = \textnormal{cost}(C_i,A') - \textnormal{cost}(C_i, a_i) \tag{For $j \neq i$,  $\textnormal{cost}(C_j, A) = \textnormal{cost}(C_j, A') = \textnormal{cost}(C_j,a_j)$}\\
        & \leq \textnormal{cost}(C_i, a_j) - \textnormal{cost}(C_i, a_i) \tag{$\textnormal{cost}(p,a_j) \geq \textnormal{cost}(p, A')$ since $a_j \in A'$}\\
        & =|C_i| \cdot \textnormal{cost}(a_i, a_j)\tag{Using \Cref{lem: centroid-fact} and that $a_i$ is the centroid of $C_i$}.
    \end{align*}
    Rearranging terms proves the inequality.

\label{lem: far-cluster}
If the coreset $\Omega$ satisfies the event $\mathcal E$ (\Cref{def: event-E}), then for any set of centers $S$, any cluster $C_j$ that is far from $S$  (deterministically) satisfies  $|\textnormal{cost} (C_j,S) - \textnormal{cost}_\Omega(C_j, S)| \lesssim  \ensuremath{\varepsilon}\, \textnormal{cost}(C_j, S).$

nodes.statement: Adding and subtracting |C_j| cdot textnormalcost(a_j,S) and applying the triangle inequality we have, |textnormalcost(C_j,S)- textnormalcost_Omega(C_j,S)| leq underbrace|textnormalcost(C_j,S) - |C_j| cdot textnormalcost(a_j,S)|_Term 1 + underbrace|textnormalcost_Omega(C_j,S) - |C_j| cdot textnormalcost(a_j,S)|_Term 2 The lemma follows if bound both terms are O(ensuremathvarepsilon\, textnormalcost(C_j, S). We show this next. paragraphBounding Term 1. As the rings R_j(0), ldots, R_j(l_ensuremathtextnormalmax + 1) partition C_j, we have Term 1 leq sum_ell= 0^ell_max+1 |textnormalcost(R_j(ell), S) - |R_j(ell)| cdot textnormalcost(a_j,S)| leq sum_ell= 0^ell_max+1 sum_p in R_j(ell) |textnormalcost(p,S) - textnormalcost(a_j,S)|. We start by bounding the term corresponding to points in R_j(l_ensuremathtextnormalmax + 1). These points are at most ensuremathvarepsilon |C_j| in number and therefore are easily dealt with. Let p be a point in R_j(l_ensuremathtextnormalmax +1). nodes.statement: Let us denote psi_T(Omega, S) = leftlvert sum_j in J_S(textnormalcost(C_j, S) - textnormalcost_Omega(C_j,S))rightrvert. Our goal is to show that \[mathopE_Omega sup_S psi_T(Omega, S) lesssim ensuremathvarepsilon textnormalcost(P,A).\] This will follow directly from the following simple bounds. Fix a set Omega and a set of centers S. For any cluster C_j with j in J_S, it always holds that (i) textnormalcost(C_j, S) lesssim tfracensuremathvarepsilonk textnormalcost(P,A) and (ii) textnormalcost_Omega(C_j, S) lesssim textnormalcost(P,A). Moreover if Omega satisfies event E, we have the stronger bound (iii) textnormalcost_Omega(C_j, S) lesssim tfracensuremathvarepsilonk textnormalcost(P,A). Let us first see how this claim directly implies the result. For any S, we trivially have \[psi_T(Omega, S) leq sum_j in J_S(textnormalcost(C_j, S) + textnormalcost_Omega(C_j, S)). \] If Omega satisfies the event E, then plugging the bounds (i) and (iii) in Claim for each jin J_S, we get that psi_T(Omega, S)lesssim ensuremathvarepsilon textnormalcost(P,A). If Omega does not satisfy E, the worst case bound (ii) in Claim gives textnormalcost_Omega(C_j, S) lesssim textnormalcost(P,A) and hence psi_T(Omega, S)lesssim k textnormalcost(P,A). Using these bounds on psi_T(Omega, S), and as ensuremathtextnormalPr[E] geq (1 - ensuremathvarepsilon/k) by Creflem:E, the Law of total Expectation gives that mathopE_Omega sup_S psi_T(Omega, S) &= mathopE_Omega sup_S [psi_T(Omega, S)| E] cdot ensuremathtextnormalPr[E] + mathopE_Omega sup_S[psi_T(Omega, S)| overlineE] cdot ensuremathtextnormalPr[overlineE] \\ &leq ensuremathvarepsilon textnormalcost(P,A) cdot 1 + ktextnormalcost(P,A) cdot tfracensuremathvarepsilonk lesssim ensuremathvarepsilon textnormalcost(P,A), as desired. We now prove Crefclm: useful-tiny. [Proof of Crefclm: useful-tiny] For any point p in C_j, using the triangle inequality (Creffact: triangle) and that C_j is close to S (so that textnormalcost(a_j,S)leq Delta_j ensuremathvarepsilon^-2) gives textnormalcost(p,S) &leq 2(textnormalcost(p,a_j) + textnormalcost(a_j,S)) leq 2(textnormalcost(p,a_j) + Delta_j ensuremathvarepsilon^-2). Let us denote $\psi_T(\Omega, S) = \left\lvert \sum_{j \in J_S}(\textnormal{cost}(C_j, S) - \textnormal{cost}_\Omega(C_j,S))\right\rvert$.  
Our goal is to show that
\[\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{\Omega} \sup_{S} \psi_T(\Omega, S) \lesssim \ensuremath{\varepsilon} \textnormal{cost}(P,A).\]
This will follow directly from the following simple bounds. 
\begin{claim}\label{clm: useful-tiny}
    Fix a set $\Omega$ and a set of centers $S$. For any cluster $C_j$ with $j \in J_S$, it always holds that (i)   $\textnormal{cost}(C_j, S) \lesssim \tfrac{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{k} \textnormal{cost}(P,A)$  and (ii)  $\textnormal{cost}_\Omega(C_j, S) \lesssim  \textnormal{cost}(P,A)$.
  
    Moreover if $\Omega$ satisfies event $\mathcal{E}$, we have the stronger bound (iii)  $\textnormal{cost}_\Omega(C_j, S) \lesssim \tfrac{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{k} \textnormal{cost}(P,A)$.
\end{claim}

Let us first see how this claim directly implies the result.

For any $S$, we trivially have
\[\psi_T(\Omega, S) \leq \sum_{j \in J_S}(\textnormal{cost}(C_j, S) + \textnormal{cost}_\Omega(C_j, S)). \]

If $\Omega$ satisfies the event $\mathcal{E}$, then plugging the bounds (i) and (iii) in Claim \ref{clm: useful-tiny} for each $j\in J_S$, we get that $\psi_T(\Omega, S)\lesssim \ensuremath{\varepsilon} \textnormal{cost}(P,A)$.

If $\Omega$ does not satisfy $\mathcal{E}$, the worst case bound (ii) in Claim \ref{clm: useful-tiny} gives $\textnormal{cost}_\Omega(C_j, S) \lesssim \textnormal{cost}(P,A)$ and hence $\psi_T(\Omega, S)\lesssim k \textnormal{cost}(P,A)$. 


Using these bounds on $\psi_T(\Omega, S)$, and as $\ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\mathcal{E}] \geq (1 - \ensuremath{\varepsilon}/k)$  by \Cref{lem:E}, the Law of total Expectation gives that 
\begin{align*}
\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{\Omega} \sup_{S} \psi_T(\Omega, S) &= \mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{\Omega} \sup_{S} [\psi_T(\Omega, S)| \mathcal{E}] \cdot \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\mathcal{E}] + \mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{\Omega} \sup_{S}[\psi_T(\Omega, S)| \overline{\mathcal{E}}] \cdot \ensuremath{\textnormal{Pr}}[\overline{\mathcal{E}}] 
\\
&\leq \ensuremath{\varepsilon} \textnormal{cost}(P,A) \cdot 1 + k\textnormal{cost}(P,A) \cdot \tfrac{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{k} \lesssim \ensuremath{\varepsilon} \textnormal{cost}(P,A),
\end{align*}
as desired.

We now prove \Cref{clm: useful-tiny}.
\begin{proof}[Proof of \Cref{clm: useful-tiny}]
For any point $p \in C_j$, using the triangle inequality (\Cref{fact: triangle}) and that $C_j$ is close to $S$ (so that $\textnormal{cost}(a_j,S)\leq \Delta_j \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^{-2})$ gives 
\begin{align}\label{eq: tiny3}
\textnormal{cost}(p,S) &\leq 2(\textnormal{cost}(p,a_j) + \textnormal{cost}(a_j,S))
\leq 2(\textnormal{cost}(p,a_j) + \Delta_j \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^{-2}).
\end{align}
Summing this over points $p$ in $C_j$ and using that $\textnormal{cost}(C_j, A) \leq T = \tfrac{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}^3}{k} \textnormal{cost}(P,A)$, we get
\begin{align*}\label{eq: tiny4}
    \textnormal{cost}(C_j,S) \leq 2 (\textnormal{cost}(C_j,A) + \textnormal{cost}(C_j,A) \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^{-2}) \leq 4 \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^{-2}\textnormal{cost}(C_j,A) \lesssim \tfrac{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{k} \textnormal{cost}(P,A). 
\end{align*}
This proves the bound (i). 

To prove the bound (ii), summing \Cref{eq: tiny3} over points in $C_j \cap \Omega$ gives,
\begin{align*}
    \textnormal{cost}_\Omega(C_j, S) &\leq 2 \sum_{p \in C_j \cap \Omega} (w_p \textnormal{cost}(p,a_j)) + 2\Delta_j \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^{-2} \sum_{p \in C_j \cap \Omega} w_p\\
    &\overset{(i)}{\leq} 2 \sum_{p \in C_j \cap \Omega} (\tfrac{3\textnormal{cost}(P,A)}{m\cdot \textnormal{cost}(p,a_j)} \cdot \textnormal{cost}(p,a_j)) + 2\Delta_j \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^{-2} \sum_{p \in C_j \cap \Omega} \tfrac{4k|C_j|}{m} \tag{By \Cref{lem: weight-bound}}\\
    &\leq 6 \textnormal{cost}(P,A) + 8k\ensuremath{\varepsilon}^{-2} \textnormal{cost}(C_j,A) \lesssim \textnormal{cost}(P,A). \tag{As $\textnormal{cost}(C_j, A) \leq \tfrac{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}^3}{k} \textnormal{cost}(P,A)$}
\end{align*}
\allowdisplaybreaks
If the event $\mathcal{E}$ holds, then step $(i)$ above can be tightened using the inequalities: $\sum_{p \in C_j \cap \Omega} w_p \textnormal{cost}(p,a_j) = \textnormal{cost}_\Omega(C_j, A) \leq (1+\ensuremath{\varepsilon}) \textnormal{cost}(C_j, A)$ which holds by property $P_3$ (see \Cref{def: event-E} of event $\mathcal{E}$) and $\sum_{p \in C_j \cap \Omega} w_p \leq (1+\ensuremath{\varepsilon}) |C_j|$ which holds by property $P_1$. 
This gives, 
\begin{align*}
    \textnormal{cost}_\Omega(C_j, S) &\leq 2(1+\ensuremath{\varepsilon}) \textnormal{cost}(C_j,A) + 2\Delta_j \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^{-2} (1+\ensuremath{\varepsilon}) |C_j|\\
    & \lesssim \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^{-2} \textnormal{cost}(C_j,A) 
    \lesssim \frac{\ensuremath{\varepsilon}}{k} \textnormal{cost}(P,A).\qedhere
\end{align*}
\end{proof}

nodes.name: Proof of  \Cref{lem: net-lemma-signature}
nodes.statement: For each i in [k], let M_alpha,i be the set of vectors given by Creflem: single-center-net. We define M'_alpha = \min(v^(1), ldots, v^(k)) | (v^(1), ldots, v^(k)) in M_alpha,1 times cdots times M_alpha,k\ where min denotes the coordinate-wise minimum of vectors. Next, we will ensure that the only non-zero coordinates correspond to points from B(S) (clusters with band b and type t). We achieve this by ``guessing'' which clusters are in B(S) and zero out the coordinates of points in the remaining clusters. Formally, for each vector v in M'_alpha and each subset C_0 of clusters \C_1, ldots, C_k\, define v(C_0) in ensuremathR^m as follows: for q_i in Omega if q_i lies in a cluster in C_0, set (v(C_0))_i = v_i; otherwise set (v(C_0))_i = 0. Let M_alpha be the set of all vectors v(C_0) obtained by varying v over points in M'_alpha and C_0 over all subsets of \C_1, ldots, C_k\. It follows that: |M_alpha| = 2^k cdot |M'_alpha| = 2^k cdot Pi_i in [k] |M_alpha,i| = exp(O(min(k2^t alpha^-2, N + k alpha^-2) cdot log(k ensuremathvarepsilon^-1 alpha^-1))). We conclude by proving that M_alpha satisfies the properties required by Crefdef: clustering-nets. Consider a set S =\x_1, ldots, x_k\ of centers from T. Let v^(j) be the vector in M_alpha,j corresponding to S and define u_min =min(v^(1), ldots, v^(k)). Finally, let u be the vector obtained by setting the i-th coordinate of u_min to zero if q_i is not in B(S). By the construction above, u is contained in M_alpha. We claim that u approximates the cost of points in Omega as required. First, if q_i notin B(S) then u_i = 0. On the other hand, if q_i in B(S), then by Creflem: single-center-net, u_i geq textnormalcost(q_i,S) - alpha cdot textnormalerr(q_i,S). Moreover if x_j in S is the nearest center to q_i, then u_i = min_j' v^(j')_i leq v^(j)_i leq textnormalcost(q_i,S)+alpha cdot textnormalerr(q_i,S) completing the proof of the lemma.

For each $i \in [k]$, let $M_{\alpha,i}$ be the set of vectors given by \Cref{lem: single-center-net}. We define $$M'_{\alpha} = \{\min(v^{(1)}, \ldots, v^{(k)}) | (v^{(1)}, \ldots, v^{(k)}) \in M_{\alpha,1} \times \cdots \times M_{\alpha,k}\}$$
where $\min$ denotes the coordinate-wise minimum of vectors.

Next, we will ensure that the only non-zero coordinates correspond to points from $B(S)$ (clusters with band $b$ and type $t$). We achieve this  by ``guessing'' which clusters are in $B(S)$ and zero out the coordinates of points in the remaining clusters. Formally, for each vector $v$ in $M'_\alpha$ and each subset $\mathcal{C}_0$ of clusters $\{C_1, \ldots, C_k\}$, define $v(\mathcal{C}_0) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^m$ as follows: for $q_i \in \Omega$ if $q_i$ lies in a cluster in $\mathcal{C}_0$, set $(v(\mathcal{C}_0))_i = v_i$; otherwise set $(v(\mathcal{C}_0))_i = 0$. Let $M_{\alpha}$ be the set of all vectors $v(\mathcal{C}_0)$ obtained by varying $v$ over points in $M'_\alpha$ and $\mathcal{C}_0$ over all subsets of $\{C_1, \ldots, C_k\}$. It follows that:
\begin{align*}
    |M_{\alpha}| = 2^k \cdot |M'_\alpha| = 2^k \cdot  \Pi_{i \in [k]} |M_{\alpha,i}| = \exp(O(\min(k2^t \alpha^{-2}, N + k \alpha^{-2}) \cdot \log(k \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^{-1} \alpha^{-1}))).
\end{align*}
We conclude by proving that $M_{\alpha}$ satisfies the properties required by \Cref{def: clustering-nets}. Consider a set $S =\{x_1, \ldots, x_k\}$ of centers from $\mathcal{T}$.  Let $v^{(j)}$ be the vector in $M_{\alpha,j}$ corresponding to $S$ and define $u_{min} =\min(v^{(1)}, \ldots, v^{(k)})$. Finally, let $u$ be the vector obtained by setting the $i$-th coordinate of $u_{min}$ to zero if $q_i$ is not in $B(S)$. By the construction above, $u$ is contained in $M_{\alpha}$.  We claim that $u$ approximates the cost of points in $\Omega$ as required. First, if $q_i \notin B(S)$ then $u_i = 0$. On the other hand, if $q_i \in B(S)$, then by \Cref{lem: single-center-net}, $u_i \geq  \textnormal{cost}(q_i,S) - \alpha \cdot \textnormal{err}(q_i,S)$. Moreover if $x_j \in S$ is the nearest center to $q_i$, then $u_i = \min_{j'} v^{(j')}_i \leq v^{(j)}_i \leq \textnormal{cost}(q_i,S)+\alpha \cdot \textnormal{err}(q_i,S)$ completing the proof of the lemma.

\label{lem: warm-up}
    Let $\Omega = \{q_1, \ldots, q_m\} \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^d$ and suppose that each point $q$ in $\Omega$ has an associated threshold distance $R_q$. For $\alpha \in (0,1/2]$, there is a set $N_\alpha \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^m$ of size at most $m (3/\alpha)^d$ with the following property. For any point $x \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^d$ there is a vector $y \in N_\alpha$ that approximates costs of the points $q_i$ with respect to $x$ as follows: for $i \in [m]$,  
	\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
		\item \label{item: net-cond-1} If $\textnormal{cost}(q_i, x) \leq R_{q_i}^2$ then 
		$| y_{i} - \textnormal{cost}(q_i, x)| \leq \alpha R_{q_i}^2$
            \item \label{item: net-cond-2}If $\textnormal{cost}(q_i, x) > R_{q_i}^2$ then $y_i \geq R_{q_i}^2 - \alpha R_{q_i}^2$.

nodes.statement: For each q in Omega, consider the d-dimensional ball of radius R_q centered at this point. Let D(q) be an (alpha R_q)-net of this ball (as defined in Creflem: eps-net). By Creflem: eps-net, we have that |D(q)| leq (3/alpha)^d and that the set D(Omega) = bigcup_q' in Omega D(q') has at most m (3/alpha)^d points. For x' in D(Omega), define the cost vector y(x') in ensuremathR^m as follows: for i in [m] set y_i(x') = textnormalcost(q_i, x'). Let N_alpha be the set of all such vectors. Note that N_alpha is of the claimed size. Let x be a point in ensuremathR^d and x' be the point in D(Omega) nearest to x. We show that y(x') in N_alpha satisfies both Crefitem: net-cond-1 and Crefitem: net-cond-2 for the point x. Proof of Crefitem: net-cond-1. If q_i in Omega is a point satisfying textnormalcost(q_i,x) leq R_q_i^2 then we have by our choice of x' that normx - x' leq alpha R_q_i. By triangle inequality (Creffact: triangle), |textnormalcost(q_i,x) - y_i(x')| &= |textnormalcost(q_i,x) - textnormalcost(q_i,x')| leq 2sqrttextnormalcost(q_i,x) textnormalcost(x,x') + textnormalcost(x,x') \\ &leq 2 sqrtR_q_i^2 cdot alpha^2 R_q_i^2 + alpha^2 R_q_i^2 leq 3alpha R_q_i^2. Proof of Crefitem: net-cond-2. Suppose that q_i in Omega is a point with textnormalcost(q_i,x)> R_q_i^2. We now want to show that y_i(x') does not underestimate the cost of q_i by too much. Consider the ball of radius R_q_i centered at q_i and let p be the point in this ball nearest to x. Clearly, D(Omega) contains a point within distance (alpha R_q_i) of p. Therefore, we have normx-x' leq normp-x + alpha R_q_i. By triangle inequality, normq_i-x' &\,\,geq \,\, normq_i-x - normx - x' \,\,geq\,\,normq_i - x - normp-x - alpha R_q_i \,\,= \,\,R_q_i - alpha R_q_i where the last line uses that q_i,p,x are collinear. Therefore, y_i(x') = textnormalcost(q_i,x') geq (R_q_i - alpha R_q_i)^2 geq R_q_i^2 - 2alpha R_q_i^2. The result follows by rescaling alpha.

nodes.statement: If |Omega| = O(1/alpha^2) then we are trivially done by taking R(x) = Omega. If this is not the case, we will construct R(x) iteratively in several rounds. Let R_i denote the set R(x) in the i-th round and Pi_i denote the orthogonal projection onto the span of U_0 cup R_i. Begin by setting R_1 = \q'\ where the q' is the point in Omega nearest to x. If in the i-th round (where i geq 1) there exists a point q violating Crefeq: progress-cond, then add it to R_i to obtain R_i+1. If no such q exists, then terminate. We show that the algorithm above terminates in O(1/alpha^2) rounds. Observe first that by the Pythagorean theorem, normPi_1 x^2 = normx^2 - norm(I-Pi_1)x^2 geq normx^2 - normq' - x^2 where the last inequality used the fact that q' is in the subspace R_1. Suppose that point q in Omega violates condition 3 in round i; we show that augmenting q to the subspace significantly increases the projection of x onto it. We have: |langle q - Pi_i q, x rangle| = |langle q, x rangle - langle Pi_iq, x rangle| > alpha cdot normq - Pi_i q cdot normq' - x. For v =tfrac q - Pi_i qnormq - Pi_i q , rearranging Crefeq: v-eq we get |langle v, x rangle| > alpha normq' - x. Moreover, we have normPi_i+1 x^2 = normPi_i x^2 + langle v, x rangle ^2 > normPi_i x^2 + alpha^2 normq' - x^2. Therefore, after each round, the norm of the projection of x increases by alpha ^2 normq' - x^2. But by Creflem: proj-lower-bound and the fact that normx^2 geq normPi_i x^2, this can happen for at most O(1/alpha^2) rounds.

Let $\Omega'$ denote the set of points $\Pi q_i$ for $q_i \in \Omega$. We apply \Cref{lem: warm-up} to $\Omega'$ with $R_{\Pi q_i}^2 = O(\textnormal{cost}(q_i,A) + \Delta_{q_i} \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^{-2})$ and the ``$\alpha$'' in the lemma set to $O(\alpha \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^2)$. We pick $V_1(U)$ to be the set of vectors returned by the lemma. Next, we show that this set indeed satisfies our requirements.

    Let $y \in V_1(U)$ be the vector corresponding to the point $x_1$ (as given by \Cref{lem: warm-up}). We show that $y$ has the claimed properties.

    \noindent \textbf{Proof of \Cref{item: term1-a}.} Suppose that $q_i$ is a point such that  $\textnormal{cost}(q_i,x_1) \leq 4 \textnormal{cost}(q_i, S) \leq 8 (\textnormal{cost}(q_i,A) + \Delta_{q_i} \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^{-2}) = R_{\Pi q_i}^2$. In this case, the squared distance between their projections onto the subspace $U$ is also at most $R_{\Pi q_i}^2$, i.e., $\norm{\Pi {q_i} - \Pi x_i}^2 \leq R_{\Pi q_i}^2$. Hence by \Cref{lem: warm-up} we obtain $|y_i - \norm{\Pi(q_i - x_1)}^2| \leq \alpha \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^2 R_{\Pi q_i}^2 \lesssim \alpha \textnormal{err}(q_i,S)$. 

    \noindent \textbf{Proof of \Cref{item: term1-b}.} If $R_{\Pi q_i}^2 \geq \norm{\Pi(q_i - x_1)}^2 \geq  \textnormal{cost}(q_i,S)$ then by the first condition of \Cref{lem: warm-up} we have that $y_i \geq \norm{\Pi(q_i - x_1)}^2 - \alpha \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^2 R_{\Pi q_i}^2 \geq  \cos(q,S) - \alpha \textnormal{err}(q_i, S)$. On the other hand, if $\norm{\Pi(q_i - x_1)}^2 \geq R_{\Pi q_i}^2$, then the second condition of \Cref{lem: warm-up} leads to the same conclusion.

    \noindent \textbf{Bounding the Net Size.} Since $U$ is a  $O(2^t\alpha^{-2})$ dimensional subspace, by \Cref{lem: warm-up} we have $|V_1(U)| = m \exp(O(2^t \alpha^{-2} \log( \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^{-1} \alpha^{-1}))) = \exp(O( 2^t \alpha^{-2} \log(k \ensuremath{\varepsilon}^{-1} \alpha^{-1})))$ where we used the fact that $|\Omega| = m= \mbox{\rm poly}(k/\ensuremath{\varepsilon})$ above.\qedhere

nodes.raw_latex:
The \emph{doubling dimension} of a metric $(X,\textnormal{dist})$ is the smallest integer $D$ such that any
ball of radius $2r$ can be covered by $2^D$ balls of radius~$r$. 

A $\gamma$-\emph{net} of $V\subset X$ is a set of points $U\subseteq V$ such that for all
$v \in V$ there is an $u \in U$ such that $\textnormal{dist}(v, u) \leq \gamma$.
nodes.clean_text: The doubling dimension of a metric (X,textnormaldist) is the smallest integer D such that any ball of radius 2r can be covered by 2^D balls of radius~r. A gamma-net of Vsubset X is a set of points Usubseteq V such that for all v in V there is an u in U such that textnormaldist(v, u) leq gamma.

nodes.name: from \cite{GuptaKL03}
nodes.statement: Let (V, textnormaldist) be a metric space with doubling dimension D and diameter Delta, and let X be a gamma-net of V. Then |X| leq 2^D cdot lceil log_2 (Delta/gamma)rceil.
assumptions: Let (V, textnormaldist) be a metric space with doubling dimension D and diameter Delta, and let X be a gamma-net of V.
conclusions: Then |X| leq 2^D cdot lceil log_2 (Delta/gamma)rceil.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{prop:doub:net}
Let $(V, \textnormal{dist})$ be a metric space with doubling dimension $D$ and diameter 
$\Delta$, and let $X$ be a $\gamma$-net of $V$. Then $|X| \leq 2^{D \cdot 
\lceil \log_2 (\Delta/\gamma)\rceil}$.
